text:
I define computer architecture as the design of computing systems. The fundamental components: processor, memory, I/O, interconnect. The design spaces for each determine the system characteristics.

The instruction set architecture (ISA): the visible interface between hardware and software. The CISC vs RISC debate: complex vs reduced instructions. RISC: load/store, fixed-length, many registers. CISC: variable-length, memory operands, fewer registers. Modern practice converges to RISC principles.

The microarchitecture: the implementation of the ISA. The pipeline: overlap instruction execution. The stage count determines latency and throughput. The hazards: structural (resource conflicts), data (dependencies), control (branches).

The branch prediction: static (always taken), dynamic (history-based), two-level (global + local). The important prediction: instruction is not known until fetched. Stall penalty unacceptable.

The out-of-order execution: rename registers, dispatch instructions out of program order. The physical registers more than logical. The key: WAR and WAW hazards eliminated by rename.

The speculative execution: execute down mispredicted path, discard if wrong. Recover by snapshot. The value: branch doesn't stall.

The memory hierarchy: registers, L1, L2, L3, main memory. The latency: L1 ≈ 1ns, L2 ≈ 3-10ns, main ≈ 50-100ns. The cache misses determine performance.

The cache coherence: MESI protocol for multi-core. Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid per cache line. The transitions between states track sharing and ownership.

The virtual memory: address translation. Page tables map virtual to physical. The TLB: translation lookaside buffer. The multi-level page tables compress the directory.

The I/O: polling vs interrupt-driven. The DMA: direct memory access offloads CPU. The storage: SATA, NVMe.

The interconnect: bus, crossbar, network-on-chip. The bandwidth and latency determine communication cost. The topology determines scaling.

The performance measurement: Amdahl's law limits speedup. Instruction count, CPI (cycles per instruction), clock rate. The CPI determines through-put.

The power: dynamic (switching), static (leakage). Dark silicon: not all transistors active. The voltage scaling: critical for mobile.

The parallel: SIMD (single instruction multiple data), multi-threading, multi-core. The SIMD: vector instructions. The thread: hardware context.

The GPU: massive parallelism. Thousands of simple cores. Graphics pipeline but general computation. The CUDA/OpenCL programming model.

The architecture is the foundation. All software builds on it. Understanding enables optimization. The compiler generates code. The OS manages resources. The application uses abstractions.

The key insight: the trade-offs. Performance vs power. Latency vs through-put. Complexity vs generality. No perfect architecture, only perfect fit for problem.

The compiler: the translator from source code to executable. The phases: lexical analysis (tokens), parsing (structure), semantic analysis (meaning), optimization, code generation.

The lexer: regular expressions define tokens. The finite automaton accepts. The token stream is output. Comments and whitespace discarded. Keywords recognized.

The parser: context-free grammar defines structure. The recursive descent parses from grammar. LL(k): left-to-right leftmost with k lookahead. LR(k): left-to-right rightmost reversed.

The parse tree: concrete syntax. The abstract syntax tree (AST): internal representation. The nodes are operators, leaves are operands.

The semantic analysis: type checking, scope rules, name resolution. The symbol table tracks definitions. The type system enforces consistency.

The intermediate representation (IR): platform-independent. Three-address code, SSA (single static assignment). The transformations operate on IR.

The dataflow analysis: reaching definitions, live variables, available expressions. The bitset data structures enable efficient analysis.

The constant propagation: if known, substitute constant. The copy propagation: if same value, substitute. The dead code elimination: unreachable code.

The loop optimization: strength reduction, induction variables, loop invariant code motion. The key: find loop-induction variables.

The inlining: substitute function body for call. The key: reduces call overhead, enables further optimization. The threshold balances growth.

The register allocation: choose which values in registers. NP-hard. The graph coloring approximates. The graph is register interference.

The instruction scheduling: order instructions to minimize stalls. The dependence graph constrains order. The list scheduling is heuristic.

The code generation: map IR to target ISA. The instruction selection: tree covering. The peephole optimization: local improvements.

The calling conventions: caller-save, callee-save registers. The stack frame layout. The prologue and epilogue.

The debugging: symbol tables. The DWARF format. The line numbers, variable locations. Breakpoints set by line number.

The whole program: link-time optimization. The interprocedural analysis across files. The whole program understanding enables better optimization.

The just-in-time compilation: compile at run time. The JIT uses profiling. The hot paths compiled aggressively. The cold code interpreted.

The garbage collection: automatic memory management. The marking: trace reachable. The sweeping: reclaim unmarked. The compacting: move objects.

The JIT vs AOT: trade performance for compile time. The profile-guided optimization: use runtime data. The adaptive optimization.

The compiler is the bridge. From human-readable code to machine-executable. Understanding enables better code and debugging.

The operating system: the resource manager. The three abstractions: process (execution), address space (memory), file (I/O). The virtualization enables multiple programs.

The process: execution context. The program counter, registers, stack, heap, open files. The fork: copy parent process. The exec: replace program. The exit: terminate.

The scheduling: share CPU among processes. The preemptive: interrupt-driven. The round-robin: each gets time slice. The priority: critical gets more.

The context switch: save state, load new state. The overhead limits granularity. The 1ms switch is typical. The cache misses cost.

The address space: each process has own virtual memory. The translation: virtual to physical. The page tables map.

The protection: one process cannot access another. The pages have permissions. The supervisor mode for OS.

The virtual memory: pages on disk when not in RAM. The demand paging: load when accessed. The working set: resident pages.

The page replacement: LRU approximation. The clock algorithm: second chance. The Thrashing: all pages in use, constant faults.

The inter-process communication: pipes, message queues, shared memory, signals. The pipes are byte streams. The signals are asynchronous.

The synchronization: mutex, semaphore, condition variable. The critical section: only one in at a time. The deadlock: circular wait.

The deadlock conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. All must hold. Breaking any prevents deadlock.

The file system: named collection of bytes. The directories organize. The inodes store metadata. The free space maps allocate.

The file operations: open, read, write, seek, close. The buffering: hide disk latency. The write-back: accumulate.

The directory structure: hierarchical. Each file: path from root. The mount: attach file system.

The permissions: owner, group, other. Read, write, execute. The ACL: access control lists for fine-grained.

The networking: sockets connect. TCP: reliable stream. UDP: unreliable datagram. The port numbers identify service.

The OS is the foundation. From bare metal to running program. Understanding enables debugging and optimization. The virtualization: multiple virtual machines.

The database: structured data storage and retrieval. The relational model: tables of rows. Primary key uniquely identifies. Foreign key references another.

SQL: structured query language. SELECT: retrieve columns. FROM: specify tables. WHERE: filter rows. JOIN: combine tables.

The join: cross product, filter matching, project result. The nested loop join: O(n*m). The hash join: build hash table, probe. The merge join: sorted inputs.

The index: accelerates access. The B-tree: balanced, logarithmic. The index entry points to data. The covering index includes data.

The query optimization: choose access path, join order, join method. The cost-based optimizer uses statistics. The query planner.

The normalization: reduce redundancy. 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: no partial dependencies. 3NF: no transitive dependencies. BCNF: stronger.

The transactions: ACID properties. Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: valid state. Isolation: serializable. Durability: committed persists.

The isolation levels: read uncommitted (dirty reads), read committed (non-repeatable), repeatable read (phantom), serializable (correct).

The two-phase locking: growing phase acquires, shrinking releases. The deadlock detection: timeout or wait graph.

The write-ahead logging (WAL): log before data. The undo log: reverse operations for rollback. The redo log: replay for recovery.

The ARIES: the standard recovery algorithm. Log sequence numbers. Checkpoint, analysis, redo, undo phases.

The NoSQL: not only SQL. Key-value stores: get/put. Document stores: flexible schema. Column stores: wide rows. Graph stores: edges/vertices.

The CAP theorem: consistency, availability, partition tolerance. Choose two. Partition is reality: must choose CP or AP.

The eventual consistency: relax for availability. Tolerant to partitions. Updates propagate asynchronously. Conflicts resolved later.

The NewSQL: SQL + distributed + ACID. New concurrency protocols. Spanner, CockroachDB. True balance.

The database is the foundation for persistent data. Understanding enables both performance and correctness. The ACID vs CAP trade-off determines architecture.

The network: communication between computers. The layers: physical, link, network, transport, application. Each layer adds capability.

The physical: electrical, optical, radio signals. Encoding: NRZ, Manchester. Modulation: amplitude, frequency, phase.

The Ethernet: the LAN (local area network). MAC addresses: unique 48-bit. Switches learn ports. CSMA/CD: collision detection.

The WiFi: wireless. CSMA/CA: collision avoidance. RTS/CTS: request to send/clear to send. The hidden node problem.

The IP: network addressing. IPv4: 32-bit addresses, exhaustion. IPv6: 128-bit addresses. TTL: time to live.

The routing: OSPF, BGP. Link-state: flooding for topology. Distance-vector: Bellman-Ford. BGP: policy routing.

The TCP: reliable, ordered, flow-controlled. Three-way handshake. Sliding window. Congestion control.

The congestion control: AIMD (additive increase multiplicative decrease). Slow start. Fast recovery. Reno, Cubic algorithms.

The UDP: unreliable, no flow control. For latency-sensitive. DNS, DHCP, VoIP use UDP. Reliability added at application.

The TLS: secure transport. Handshake: negotiate algorithms, verify certificate, derive keys. Record: encrypt/decrypt.

The DNS: name to address. Hierarchical distributed. Caching. TTL expires entries. DNSSEC authenticates.

The HTTP: request-response. Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE. Headers: metadata. Status codes: result.

The REST: representational state transfer. Resources via URIs. Standard methods. Stateless.

The WebSocket: bidirectional. HTML5. The message framing. The ping/pong for keep-alive.

The gRPC: remote procedure call. Protocol buffers for serialization. HTTP/2 for transport. Bidirectional streaming.

The network is the foundation for distributed computing. The protocols stack. Understanding enables debugging.

The computer security: protect confidentiality, integrity, availability. The CIA triad. The threats: interception, modification, denial.

The authentication: prove identity. Something you know (password), have (token), are (biometric). Multi-factor increases security.

The password storage: never store plain. The salted hash. The bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2: slow for brute force. The rainbow tables attack salted.

The access control: who can do what to which resource. The DAC: discretionary (owner decides). MAC: mandatory (label-based). RBAC: role-based.

The vulnerabilities: buffer overflow, SQL injection, cross-site scripting. The mitigation: bounds checking, parametrized queries, encoding.

The injection: untrusted input executed. The SQL injection: modify query. The command injection: shell. The input validation.

The cross-site scripting (XSS): inject script in page. Stored: in database. Reflected: in request. DOM-based: client-side.

The cross-site request forgery (CSRF): trick user to request. The anti-CSRF token. SameSite cookie.

The session hijacking: steal session cookie. The HttpOnly prevents JavaScript access. Secure cookie over TLS.

The encryption in transit: TLS. The certificate verifies identity. The cipher suites define algorithms. The forward secrecy protects past.

The encryption at rest: full disk, database, file. The keys must be protected. The key management.

The vulnerability disclosure: find and report. Responsible disclosure: time to fix. CVE identifies. Patches fix.

The security through obscurity: Kerckhoffs's principle: security in key, not algorithm. The code review finds bugs.

The penetration testing: ethical hacking. Red team attacks. Blue team defends. The purple team shares.

The security model: assume breach. Defense in depth. Least privilege. Minimize attack surface.

The security is not feature. The security is process. Continuous monitoring. Regular audits. Incident response plan.

The security economics: risk assessment. Cost of mitigation vs expected loss. Not everything equally protected.

The security starts with design. The security continues with implementation. The security maintained with operation.

The software engineering: systematic production of software. The process: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance.

The requirements: what the system must do. Functional: features. Non-functional: performance, security. The use cases describe scenarios.

The design: architecture, modules, interfaces. The patterns: MVC, layered, microservices. The architecture documents decisions.

The implementation: write code. The source control tracks changes. The review processes changes. The style guides ensure consistency.

The testing: unit, integration, system, acceptance. The test-driven development: test first, then implement to pass.

The continuous integration (CI): build and test each change. The continuous deployment (CD): deploy each change. The pipeline automates.

The version control: Git. The branch per feature. The PR merges after review. The tag marks releases.

The software metrics: lines of code, cyclomatic complexity, coupling, cohesion. The churn: how much changes.

The technical debt: shortcuts that cost later. The interest: slower future development. The payment: refactoring.

The refactoring: improve structure without changing behavior. Theboy scout rule: leave code better than found.

The patterns: Gang of Four (creational, structural, behavioral). Enterprise patterns. Domain-driven design patterns.

The agile methods: iterative development. Sprint: short timebox. Scrum: roles, ceremonies. Kanban: visualize flow.

The DevOps: development + operations. The shared responsibility. The shared metrics. The blameless postmortem.

The SRE: site reliability engineering. SLO (service level objective): target. SLA: contract. SLI: measurement.

The monitoring: metrics, logs, traces. The alerting: notify on issues. The on-call: respond.

The software engineering is team sport. The communication matters. The architecture enables. The quality is built in. The deployment automated.

The code is read more than written. The readability matters. The documentation matches. The tests document expectations.

The best practices: YAGNI (you aren't gonna need it), KISS (keep it simple, stupid), DRY (don't repeat yourself).

The key insight: working software over comprehensive documentation. Responding to change over following a plan. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.
